title: Paul’s Farewell to Ephesus
overview: Acts 20 details Paul’s travels and his heartfelt farewell to the Ephesian elders. After ministering in Macedonia and Greece, Paul returns to Troas, where he preaches late into the night and miraculously raises Eutychus from the dead. He then journeys toward Jerusalem, determined to fulfill his mission despite knowing the hardships ahead. At Miletus, Paul summons the elders of the Ephesian church for an emotional charge, warning them of future dangers and urging faithful shepherding of the flock. This chapter highlights Paul’s dedication, pastoral heart, and the cost of gospel ministry, emphasizing perseverance, vigilance, and God’s sustaining grace in the face of opposition.
structure:
**Verses 1-12: Paul’s Journey and Ministry in Troas.** Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, then stays in Troas where he preaches extensively, culminating in the miraculous raising of Eutychus.

**Verses 13-16: Paul’s Travel Toward Jerusalem.** Paul and his companions sail from Troas to Miletus, intentionally bypassing Ephesus to save time, as Paul is eager to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.

**Verses 17-38: Paul’s Farewell to the Ephesian Elders.** From Miletus, Paul calls the elders of the Ephesian church to give a solemn charge. He recounts his faithful ministry, warns of future threats, exhorts them to vigilance, and commends them to God’s care. The chapter closes with a deeply emotional farewell.

keyVerses.text: But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God.
keyVerses.significance: This verse captures Paul’s resolute commitment to his divine calling, emphasizing the cost and joy of faithful gospel ministry. It highlights the central theme of perseverance despite suffering.

keyVerses.text: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
keyVerses.significance: Paul’s charge to the Ephesian elders underscores the sacred responsibility of church leadership. It affirms the church’s divine purchase through Christ’s blood and the need for vigilant pastoral care.

keyVerses.text: Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals Paul’s intense pastoral concern and tireless dedication to warning and nurturing the believers, modeling shepherd-like vigilance and love.

keyVerses.text: And upon the first day of the week, when the disciples came together to break bread, Paul preached unto them, ready to depart on the morrow; and continued his speech until midnight.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the early Christian practice of gathering on the first day of the week for fellowship and teaching, and Paul’s earnest commitment to instructing the church.

characters.name: Paul
characters.description: The apostle and central figure of the chapter, Paul is depicted as a devoted missionary and pastor. He travels extensively, preaches boldly, raises Eutychus from the dead, and gives a poignant farewell to the Ephesian elders, exemplifying faithful ministry and sacrificial leadership.

characters.name: Eutychus
characters.description: A young man who falls asleep during Paul’s long sermon in Troas and falls from a third-story window. Paul’s miraculous intervention brings him back to life, symbolizing God’s power and care over His people.

characters.name: Elders of Ephesus
characters.description: The leaders of the Ephesian church summoned by Paul at Miletus. They receive Paul’s solemn charge to shepherd the church faithfully and to be vigilant against false teachers and internal threats.

characters.name: Holy Ghost
characters.description: Mentioned as the one who appoints overseers and testifies about Paul’s coming sufferings. The Spirit’s role affirms divine guidance and empowerment in church leadership and ministry.

themes.description: Paul’s example of tireless preaching, teaching, and pastoral care demonstrates the call to serve God with humility, perseverance, and love, even in the face of opposition and suffering.
The chapter emphasizes the responsibility of elders to watch over and feed the flock, guarding against false teachers and caring for the spiritual wellbeing of the church.
Paul’s journey and ministry are under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, who warns him of coming trials and appoints leaders, showing God’s sovereign control over the spread of the gospel.
Paul’s emotional farewell reflects deep pastoral love and the cost of gospel ministry, encouraging believers to remain faithful despite impending separation and hardship.

historicalContext: Acts 20 occurs during Paul’s third missionary journey, approximately AD 57, in the Roman province of Asia Minor and surrounding regions. The cities mentioned—Macedonia, Greece, Troas, Miletus, and Ephesus—were important centers of early Christianity and commerce. Travel was often by ship along the Mediterranean coast, and journeys could be perilous and lengthy. The early church met in homes or upper rooms, as seen in Troas, reflecting the informal yet committed nature of Christian gatherings. Jewish opposition to Paul’s ministry was common, as noted by the plots against him, reflecting tensions between emerging Christian communities and established religious authorities. The political environment was under Roman rule, which allowed relative freedom for missionary activity but also posed risks of imprisonment and persecution.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes Paul’s perseverance as an example of God’s sustaining grace and sovereign calling. The charge to elders is seen as a divine mandate for church governance and the protection of doctrinal purity.

Dispensationalists highlight the distinct role of the church age and Paul’s missionary efforts as foundational for the present dispensation. Paul’s warnings about false teachers are interpreted as ongoing challenges for the church until Christ’s return.

Early church fathers viewed Paul’s farewell as a model of pastoral care and apostolic authority. They often emphasized the spiritual oversight of elders and the importance of guarding the church against heresy.

crossReferences.connection: Paul’s declaration of finishing his course with joy in Acts 20:24 parallels his later testimony of having fought the good fight and kept the faith.
Peter’s exhortation to elders to shepherd the flock willingly echoes Paul’s charge in Acts 20:28 to feed the church of God.
Jesus as the Good Shepherd provides the theological foundation for Paul’s call to elders to shepherd the church purchased by Christ’s blood.
The admonition to obey church leaders who watch over souls connects to Paul’s warnings and instructions to the Ephesian elders.
Paul’s willingness to face death for Christ’s sake in Acts 20:24 resonates with his statement that to live is Christ and to die is gain.

application: Commit to faithful and humble service in ministry, following Paul’s example of perseverance despite hardships.
Church leaders should vigilantly shepherd their congregations, guarding against false teachings and caring deeply for believers.
Believers are encouraged to gather regularly for fellowship, teaching, and breaking of bread, fostering spiritual growth and unity.
Trust in God’s sovereign guidance and strength when facing trials or uncertainty in ministry or personal life.
Practice sacrificial love and be willing to say difficult goodbyes for the sake of the gospel’s advancement.
Support and care for the weak within the church community, remembering the blessing of giving over receiving.
conclusion: Acts 20 stands as a powerful testament to the heart of apostolic ministry—marked by unwavering commitment, pastoral love, and reliance on the Holy Spirit. Paul’s journey, preaching, and farewell charge to the Ephesian elders encapsulate the challenges and joys of serving Christ’s church. His warnings and encouragement continue to resonate, calling believers and leaders alike to vigilance, faithfulness, and sacrificial care. This chapter invites Christians today to embrace God’s calling with courage, shepherd His flock with diligence, and trust in His grace amid trials.
timeline: c. AD 57 - Paul’s Third Missionary Journey

definitions.definition: An earnest urging or encouragement to do something, especially in a spiritual or moral context.
Spiritual leaders appointed to oversee and shepherd the local church, responsible for teaching, governance, and care.
A biblical metaphor for the community of believers, emphasizing their need for pastoral care and protection.
Another term for elders or bishops, those who watch over and guide the church under the Holy Spirit’s direction.
A Jewish festival occurring fifty days after Passover, significant in Christian tradition as the day the Holy Spirit was poured out on believers.
